en: A Brief Explanation of Master Xuanzang of the Tang Dynasty’s “True Proof of Consciousness-Only,” excerpted from the *Zongjing Lu* (Record of the Mirror of the Source) by Chan Master Yongming Yanshou of the Song Dynasty,
with a brief commentary by Ming Dynasty Master Ouyi Zhixu.

The text is divided into three sections: first, the introduction; second, the main exposition; third, the concluding praise. Within the first section, there are two parts: first, the direct narration;
second, the citation of evidence. This is the first [part].

Regarding the "True Valid Cognition of Consciousness-Only": this refers to the Great Tang Tripiṭaka Master, who, at the city of Kanyākubja in Central India, established a formal syllogism (*prayoga*) before King Śīlāditya during an eighteen-day *aviśeṣa-mahāpariṣad* (unrestricted great assembly).

He extensively summoned śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas from the five regions of India who were learned in the meaning of the Dharma, as well as followers of the Hīnayāna and non-Buddhists, to serve as his opponents. He then set forth a single logical argument.
The writing was inscribed upon a golden tablet. After eighteen days had passed, not a single person dared to refute it.
△ Second, the citation of evidence:

Thus, the *Yinming shu* (Commentary on the Nyāyapraveśa) states: "For instance, when the Great Master traveled throughout the Western Regions and was about to return with his studies complete, at that time King Śīlāditya..."
O King, the King of the Five Indias established an eighteen-day unrestricted great assembly (aṣṭādaśa-dina-avārṣika-mahāpariṣad) and commanded the Great Master to establish his doctrine.

He sent forth [the Master] to travel throughout India to select the wise and virtuous, all of whom gathered at the site of the assembly. There, he dispatched the non-Buddhists and followers of the Hīnayāna to compete in raising challenges and objections.
The Great Master established the formal syllogism (*pramāṇa*), and none dared to respond to it.

△ Second, the explicit exposition has three parts: first, the actual presentation of the three members; second, the questions and answers outlining the topical divisions; third, the detailed explanation according to those divisions.
Now, the first part.

The Great Master established the following inference for the Cognition-Only (Vijñaptimātra) doctrine: **Thesis:** Truly, that which is commonly acknowledged as form (*rūpa*) is necessarily not separate from eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
**Reason:** Because it is admitted by [the opponent] itself to be included within the first three [categories] while not being included among the eyes. **Similar Example:** Like eye-consciousness.
**Application:** All things included within the first three categories that are not included among the eyes are not separate from eye-consciousness; the similar example is like the eye [itself].
Consciousness. A dissimilar example is the visual faculty (cakṣur-indriya).
△ Second, the question-and-answer section outlining the topical divisions.

Question: Why is the phrase "as admitted by oneself" not included? Answer: It is not a valid reason (*hetu*); it is merely a preliminary statement used at the outset of the reason to provide a distinction.

[This is] a refutation. Furthermore, it is not that the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) does not accept [the Mahāyāna], nor is it something the Mahāyāna itself admits. This is because the reason (*hetu*) functions upon a factual basis (*dharmin*), and all three members [of the syllogism] are common [to both systems].

First, the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*) are clarified; subsequently, questions and answers are presented. The initial section has two parts: first, the demonstration of the thesis; second, the explanation of the reason.
In this section, first the question and answer are presented, followed by the topical outline (*kośasthāna*). The question asks:

"Since the phrase 'admitted by oneself' (*svayaṃ-īṣṭa*) already appears in the reason (*hetu*), why is this phrase not used in the application (*upanaya*)? The answer states: "The phrase 'admitted by oneself' is not the actual correct reason;

it is merely a provisional expression used at the beginning of the reason to exclude potential faults. Furthermore, it does not mean that what is not admitted by the Hīnayāna is 'admitted by oneself' in the Mahāyāna."

However, when the reason—"because it is included within these first three [realms] yet not included by the eye"—is applied to the subject (*dharmin*), all three members [of the syllogism] are equally common (*sādhāraṇa*) with respect to the contradictory particularity (*viśeṣaviruddha*).
Therefore, the term "admitted by oneself" (*svayam-abhyupagata*) is employed as a qualification to exclude this.

The explanation of the contradiction regarding the particularity will appear in the subsequent text. Regarding the section following the initial clarification of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*), the topical outline (*uddāna*) is self-evident.

△ Third, the detailed explanation according to the topical divisions has two parts. First, the explanation of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*). Second, the presentation of questions and answers. Within the first part, there are two sections:
first, the explanation of the thesis; second, the explanation of the reason. Within the first section, there are two subsections: first, the explanation of the locus of the thesis (*pakṣāśraya*);

second, the explanation of the essence of the thesis (*pakṣasvarūpa*). Within the first subsection, there are again two parts: first, the division of the text; second, the explanation. This is the first [part].
First, regarding the initial thesis: the five characters "because of being truly established, color" (*satyatvāt siddha-rūpa*) constitute the statement.
Of these, the single character "color" (*rūpa*) is precisely the *dharmin* (the subject), while the remaining four characters serve merely to prevent logical fallacies.
△ Second, the explanation has two parts. First, the explanation of "because it is real" (*tattvataḥ*); second, the explanation of "universally established" (*prasiddha*). Now, for the first:

regarding the two characters "real" (*zhen*) and "because" (*gu*) at the outset, they serve to prevent errors. They exclude the error of contradicting worldly consensus as well as errors such as contradicting the scriptures.

(First, excluding the error of contradicting worldly consensus: An opponent asks: "The world is shallow and superficial; one knows [things] by birth. Form (*rūpa*) is distinct from consciousness (*vijñāna*)."
[Question: There is. Now, the Mahāyāna establishes that form is not separate from visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), because it is not something commonly known by the world.

Why does this inference (*anumāna*) not commit the fallacy of contradicting worldly consensus? [Answer: Generally, when establishing an inference, there are those that are autonomous (*svatantra*), those that are for others (*paratantra*), and those that are common to both.

Each has its own specific qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) according to what is appropriate. If it is an autonomous inference, it is qualified by the phrase "admitted by oneself" (*svīkṛta*). If it is an inference for others, [it is qualified by] "you" (*bhavān*).

The term "ultimately" (*paramārthataḥ*) serves as a qualification. If it were a common inference (*sādhāraṇa-anumāna*), the term "ultimately" would not be required as a qualification; however, in this case, it is a common inference that requires such a distinction.

The phrase "because it is true" indicates that it relies upon the ultimate; specifically, it is established based on the truth of the manifestation of essence and function (*tattva-vṛtti-prabhāsana-satya*) among the four types of ultimate truths.
Regarding the subject (*dharmin*) of the thesis (*pakṣa*) established within inference (*anumāna*), there are three distinct types:

that which is established by oneself, that which is established by another, or that which is established by both oneself and another. If it is established by oneself, one distinguishes it by employing the phrase "admitted by myself" (*svīkṛta*).
If it is established by another, one distinguishes it by employing the phrase "your own tenet" (*tvad-abhimata*).
If this were established through the common consensus of both self and others, one would employ the term "ultimate" (paramārtha) to distinguish it.
Now, this single word "form" (rūpa) is a valid cognition (anumāna) established by the common consensus of both self and others;

yet, because the opponent does not realize that form is not separate from consciousness, the phrase "because it is real" (satyatvāt) is used to indicate that it relies on the ultimate sense and not on the false perceptions of ordinary people.
Regarding the four kinds of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*): First is the worldly ultimate truth, also called the truth of the manifestation of essence and function.
This refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), which differ from the self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*) clung to by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Second is the ultimate truth of principle, also called the truth of the differentiation of cause and effect. This refers to the Four Noble Truths, such as suffering (*duḥkha*), which are the reality of mundane and supramundane causes and effects.
Because it is not false or erroneous, the third is the ultimate truth of realization (*prāpti-paramārtha-satya*), also called the truth that reveals reality by relying on the true;

this refers to the suchness of the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā-tathatā*) when speaking from the perspective of the realizing wisdom. The fourth is the ultimate of the ultimate (*paramārtha-paramārtha*), also called the truth that discards the expression to discuss the intent;
this refers to the single true dharma-realm (*eka-dharmadhātu*) when speaking from the perspective of the realized principle.
(Next, refuting the fault of contradicting the teachings: Question: It may be acceptable for those who are not practitioners (*aśaikṣa*) to not contradict worldly conventions.

Furthermore, as the Blessed One permitted in the *Āgama* sūtras of the Hīnayāna that form exists apart from consciousness, and since practitioners of the Hīnayāna commonly reckon that there are real objects external to the mind, does this not contradict the teachings of the *Āgamas* and so forth for those Hīnayāna practitioners? Answer: This is merely based on the superiority of the Mahāyāna.
This is established according to the meaning. For those who study the teachings of the Hīnayāna, it is not a worldly error.
There are two kinds of "worldly" (loka): first, the non-learnerly world, which refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*);
second, the learnerly world, which refers to those who have attained the first, second, and third fruits [of the path]. The Arhat realizes the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
[The fruit] transcends the three realms; although the body has not yet perished, it is no longer subsumed within the mundane world. Furthermore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:

"If one who has truly attained arhatship does not believe in this Dharma, such a thing is impossible. Therefore, what is discussed here does not contradict those who have already attained the stage beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Those still in training (*śaikṣa*) belong to the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), which is here referred to as "those who study the Small Vehicle. △ Second, the explanation.

This is universally established (*prasiddha*). Question: The phrase "because it is real" excludes faults such as [the view held by] worldly people or those who contradict the teachings; this I have already heard.

But what fault does the term "universally established" exclude? Answer: The word "universally established" is placed [at the beginning] in order to exclude two kinds of forms that are not universally established. (What are these two?)

First: among the twenty schools of the Hīnayāna, with the exception of four schools—the Ekavyāvahārikas, the Lokottaravādins, the Prajñaptivādins, and the Kukkutikas—none of which assert that a Bodhisattva in his final existence possesses defiled form (*saṃkliṣṭa-rūpa*) nor that a Buddha possesses out-flowing form (*sāsrava-rūpa*), the remaining sixteen schools all admit that a Bodhisattva in his final existence possesses defiled form and that a Buddha possesses out-flowing form. However, the Mahāyāna does not admit this; such is the general rule.

[The first] is the ultimate; [the second] is the formation of color (rūpa). The Mahāyāna teaches that there is the color of Buddhas from other directions, whereas the Hīnayāna [teaches] that the Buddha possesses untainted (anāsrava) and sublime color.
Although the Sautrāntika school admits the existence of the physical forms (*rūpa*) of Buddhas in other directions, they do not admit that these are untainted (*anāsrava*).

Furthermore, the other nineteen schools all deny the existence of such forms; thus, this is another type of "unestablished" (*aprasiddha*) *rūpa*. Together with the previous [type], there are two types of unestablished *rūpa* (now posited).
If one does not say "established," but merely states that "true *rūpa*" is the subject (*dharmin*), it necessarily does not depart from visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).

Thesis: Furthermore, when speaking of "form" (*rūpa*), whether one grants it or does not grant it, it is entirely subsumed within the subject (*dharmin*). That which was granted by the earlier Hīnayāna is not granted by the Mahāyāna;

if one now establishes it as "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*), one commits the fault of partial non-establishment of the specifically characterized object (*sva-viśeṣya-aprasiddha*) and also commits the fault of partial contradiction with scripture. Moreover, that which is granted by the Mahāyāna is not granted by the Hīnayāna; now...
If one posits [the subject] as an existent phenomenon (*dharma*), one commits the fallacy of the "partial non-establishment of the locus" (*pakṣābhāsa*) for either the proponent or the opponent.

Furthermore, when one advances the reason "not included among the first three [bases]"—which is subsumed under the category of "not included among the bases of eye"—one commits the fallacy of the "non-establishment of the locus" for either the proponent or the opponent, because the subject previously stated lacks an established basis in the form [of the visual faculty].
Now, in order to specifically exclude these four types of fallacies, the term "established" (*prasiddha*) is employed.

As for the remaining sixteen schools, which allow that a Bodhisattva in his final existence possesses defiled matter and that a Buddha possesses out-flowing (sāsrava) matter, these are provisional teachings of the Tripiṭaka.
[According to them], during the three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas, one subdues the afflictions without severing them;
thus, while the Prince was in the royal palace, he fully experienced the superior pleasures of the five desires for ten years, and moreover, through sexual union, fathered Rāhula.
Therefore, it is said that his final body possesses defiled form (*sāsrava-rūpa*).

Furthermore, although at the time of sitting in the place of enlightenment he severed the fetters and realized untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) through thirty-four moments of mind, this *zhànglù* golden body was still produced by tainted wholesome karma;
thus, it is said that the Buddha’s body is tainted form. As for those who do not accept this in the Mahāyāna, according to the *Tongjiao* (Shared Teaching):

When a Bodhisattva reaches the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), residual afflictions (*kleśa*) have already been completely severed; what remains is merely the support for habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) that nourishes rebirth, and thus it is neither defiled nor outflowing (*sāsrava*).

In the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), one severs the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) at the first abiding (*vihāra*) and severs the afflictions of thought (*saṃjñā-kleśa*) at the seventh abiding, thereby becoming free from both defilement and outflows—how much more so then in the final birth and the stage of Buddhahood? In the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*), from the very beginning...

Faith severs [wrong] views; when faith severs [afflictions of] the realm of thought, one is then free from both defilement and outflows (*āsrava*). How much more so, then, regarding subsequent bodies and the fruit of Buddhahood!

As for the Hīnayāna not permitting the form-body (*rūpakāya*) of Buddhas in other directions, it is because the names of Buddhas in other directions are not heard within the provisional teachings (*upāyadeśanā*).
Although the Sautrāntika school permits the form-body of Buddhas in other directions, they do not permit it to be without outflows.
This person happened to hear Mahāyāna sūtras and, through faith in the Buddha’s words, came to know that there are Buddhas in other directions named [so-and-so].

Yet they still maintain that when the various Buddhas were practicing their causal conduct, they certainly did not sever their afflictions; therefore, the bodies they received remain non-outflow (*anāsrava*).

Furthermore, the nirvāṇa conceived by the Hīnayāna is merely the principle of emptiness and quiescence; therefore, all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are collectively termed "outflowing" (*sāsrava*).
They do not know that the Middle Way of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) is fully endowed with the wondrous form of the non-outflowing (*anāsrava*).

Question: Since the two characters "universally established" (*prasiddha*) exclude those forms that are not universally established for both parties, I do not yet understand which forms the Tripitaka Master establishes as "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).
Answer: Apart from those forms not universally established for both parties, all other forms accepted by both the proponent and the opponent are taken collectively as consciousness-only.
Therefore, the *Nyāyapraveśa-ṭīkā* states: "Those forms accepted by both, remaining after the two [unestablished] have been excluded."
The term "wei" (唯) refers to Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*);
it establishes the present Mahāyāna school. The term "di" (敵) refers to that Hīnayāna school. The rest may be understood.
△ Second, the explanation of the latter member of the thesis: the nature of the subject (*pakṣa*).
The proponent subsequently states that "it is certainly not separate from eye-consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*); this is an established qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Question:

Why does this not incur the fault of the qualifier being unestablished (*asiddha-viśeṣaṇa*)? For instance, among the Hīnayāna schools, who would admit that form (*rūpa*) is not separate from eye-consciousness? Answer: Regarding this term "form" (*rūpa*)...

This is merely the locus of the thesis (*pakṣāśraya*) for the proponent's own system. However, within the opponent's system, the sense of "not being separate" (*avinirbhāga*) can still be established.

This is because the Hīnayāna school accepts that visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) takes form (*rūpa*) as its object and directly grasps its essence; thus, there is the sense of "not being separate. Furthermore, they accept that the very nature of visual consciousness itself is also not separate from visual consciousness.

Therefore, there is no fault of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) being unestablished (*asiddha*). Question: Since it is accepted that visual consciousness grasps the objective form (*ālambanarūpa*), [how is this so?]

There is a sense of inseparability; when these later [elements] combine to form the body of the thesis (*pakṣa*), would there not be the fault of redundancy (*punarukta*)? Answer: There is no fault of redundancy.
In this Mahāyāna system, one merely takes the object to be inseparable from the mind, as there are no external objects that exist in reality.

If the combination of the former and latter [terms] constitutes the body of the thesis, then the proponent accepts it while the opponent does not; this mutual contention between proponent and opponent is what is called the "body of the thesis."
In this context, there is merely a dispute over the verbal expression; the underlying intention has not yet been examined.
Regarding the basis of the thesis (*pakṣāśraya*), it must be mutually accepted by reason; if it were not mutually accepted, it would not be fully established (*asiddha*).

Regarding the essence of the thesis (*pakṣasvabhāva*) itself, it too must be mutually accepted; if it were not mutually accepted, it likewise would not be fully established. If the subject (*dharmin*) in the former [statement]...
Once the thesis (*pakṣa*) has been established as a synthesis of its constituent parts, it must be such that the proponent accepts it while the opponent does not;
only when the proponent and opponent dispute it together can one avoid the fallacy of self-contradiction and thereby constitute the essence of a thesis.

Because they dispute it together, one must rely upon reasons (*hetu*) and examples (*dṛṣṭānta*) to resolve and clarify it; only then does it become a true "prover" (*sādhana*). Now, regarding this establishment of the thesis:
Within this context, since the dispute merely concerns verbal expression, it is necessary to speak of "universally established form" (*prasiddha-rūpa*).

Because the underlying intention and admission have not yet been investigated, regarding the form admitted by both schools, there is no need at present to minutely distinguish between the difference of the *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part) and the *svabhāva-rūpa* (essential nature).
This is because the essential nature of form is what both schools equally admit, whereas the image-part of form is [the position] of the Hīnayāna.
This is what [the opponent] does not permit. Now, when the Tripiṭaka master establishes his formal inference (*pramāṇa*), the words he utters refer merely to the term "form" (*rūpa*);

yet, in his intended meaning, he points specifically to the "objective aspect" (*nimittabhāga*). This intended meaning—that it is the form of the objective aspect—is only subject to the refutation by the Hīnayāna school after the reason (*hetu*) has been analyzed;
at this point, within the establishment of the thesis (*pakṣa*), it has not yet been refuted.
The "Discourse on the Thesis" (Biàn zōng) is concluded.

This is the concluding summary that explains the thesis. △ Second, the explanation of the reasons (shì yīn). Part one: first, the establishment of the outline; second, the detailed explanation. Now, the first [part].
Next, the discussion of the cause has two parts: first, clarifying the primary cause; second, explaining the use of provisional language to eliminate errors.

Part Two: The Exegesis has two sections: first, the exegesis of the primary cause; second, the exegesis of the use of provisional language to eliminate errors. Within the first section, there are again three parts.
First, the formal explanation; second, the analysis of the meaning; third, the conclusion. Now, for the first:
regarding the initial correct cause, the phrase "subsumed by the first three" means that among the eighteen *dhātus*, one takes the very first element from each of the three groups of six.
These are the eye-faculty *dhātu*, the eye-consciousness *dhātu*, and the form-object *dhātu*; these are the first three among the eighteen *dhātus*.
This is the [section on] the elements (*dhātu*).

△ Second, the analysis of the meaning, which is further divided into two parts. First, clarifying the meaning of the inclusion within the first three; second, clarifying the meaning of that which is not included by the eye.
Now, the first part.

Question: Even if one does not say "subsumed under the first three [aggregates]," but merely says "not subsumed by the eye," what further fault is there? Answer: There are two faults: first, the fault of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*);
second, the fault of contradicting one's own teaching (*sva-śāstra-virodha*). Regarding the fault of inconclusiveness:

if one were to formulate a syllogism as follows—"That which is truly established as form is necessarily not separate from visual consciousness; the reason being that it is not subsumed by the eye; the example being like visual consciousness itself"—then...
The reason "not being subsumed by the eye" (*cakṣur-asaṃgṛhīta*) is applied to the five subsequent [reasons] following the dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
Since all of these are "not subsumed by the eye," an opponent raises the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*), saying:

"Is it like visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), which, while not being subsumed by the eye, is nonetheless not separate from visual consciousness? Can this serve as proof for your claim that 'form' (*rūpa*) is not separate from visual consciousness? Or...

If the latter five and three [elements] are likewise not subsumed by the eye, yet these latter five and three are necessarily dissociated from visual consciousness, does this not prove that the "form" (rūpa) you assert as established is indeed necessarily dissociated from visual consciousness?
Question: Now, if the Mahāyāna were to say that even the latter five and three are not dissociated from visual consciousness, would that be acceptable?
Answer: Even if the Mahāyāna were to grant that the latter five and three are not dissociated from visual consciousness...

[If one were to] recognize [them as such], one would avoid the fault of violating the indeterminate [category], yet it would contradict one's own school; for within the Mahāyāna school, it is taught that the last five [faculties] and three determinate [factors] are dissociated from visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).

Therefore, [the author] specifically establishes the first three [faculties] as the basis for inclusion (the "half-reason"), precisely in order to exclude the last five and three from being included among the first three.
△ Second, clarifying the meaning of that which is not subsumed by the eye. Question:
If one merely states that [the first three elements] are subsumed [by the eye], but does not state that they are not subsumed by the eye, what fault is there? Answer: It incurs two faults:

first, the fault of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); second, the fault of contradicting the determination of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena. Regarding the inconclusive [fault]: if one were to establish...

The proof (*sādhana*) states: "That which is truly established as form (*rūpa*) is necessarily not separate from visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). The reason (*hetu*) states: "Because it is included within the first three [bases]. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is: "Just like visual consciousness.
However, this reason—being "included within the first three"—is too broad (*vyabhicāra*). It can be applied to the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), namely the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*).

To avoid the fault of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), one might say: "Is it not like visual consciousness, which, while being included within the first three, is not separate from visual consciousness? This serves as the proof.
(Regarding what you have said: Is it not the case that the universally established form (*rūpa*) is not separate from visual consciousness?

[Is it] like the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), which is also included within the first three aggregates (*skandha*), yet the visual faculty is not necessarily not separate from visual consciousness? Does this not prove that the universally established form you speak of is likewise not necessarily not separate from visual consciousness?
Question: Why do you not say "necessarily separate," but instead say "not necessarily not separate"? Answer: Because, from the perspective of the Mahāyāna, the visual faculty...
Regarding visual consciousness, it cannot be definitively determined as being either identical to or distinct from [the eye-faculty]. First, it is not distinct:

because the faculty is the cause (as that which gives rise to it) and consciousness is the effect (as that which is produced), they are not distinct due to their simultaneity. Furthermore, since the faculty is matter (*rūpa*) and consciousness is mind (*citta*), their essences are each separate;
thus, they are called "not identical. Therefore, for now, one can only say that it is not definitively non-distinct (without saying it is definitively distinct). One transgression of the law.

Regarding the fault of contradiction with the specifically characterized nature (*svalakṣaṇa*): "the specifically characterized nature of the property" refers to the specifically characterized nature of the property that constitutes the latter member of the thesis (*pakṣa*).
"Contradiction with certainty" means that the reason contradicts the thesis. The opponent sets forth a proof of contradiction as follows:

"Color, as established by ultimate truth, is a subject (dharmin) that is not non-separate from visual consciousness; this is the thesis (pakṣa). The reason (hetu) is: 'because it is included within the first three [bases].

The example (dṛṣṭānta) is: 'like the visual faculty. Thus, the opponent takes the previously cited dissimilar example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta) and treats it as a similar example (sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta), and takes the similar example and treats it as a dissimilar example.
Question: "Does this constitute a contradiction with the specific characteristic (sva-lakṣaṇa-viruddha) of the property to be proven? Answer (by the opponent): "This is not a genuine refutation."

Now, for a reason to be a "contradiction of the specific characteristic" (*svabhāvaviruddha*) of the property to be proven, it must be established that [the reason] is absent from the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and present in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), while for the opponent, it is present in the similar instances and absent in the dissimilar instances;

only then does it constitute a contradiction of the specific characteristic of the property. In the present case, both the proponent and the opponent agree that the reason is present in both the similar and dissimilar instances.
Therefore, this is not a genuine fallacy of contradiction of the specific characteristic of the property. Question: Since it is not a contradiction of the specific characteristic...
Question: Can one obtain the fallacies of *viruddha* (contradiction), *pratibādhita-viruddha* (contradiction by sublation), and *anaikāntika* (inconclusiveness)? Answer:

No. Indeed, the fallacies of *viruddha*, *pratibādhita-viruddha*, and *anaikāntika* [arise] when the proponent and opponent both dispute a single *dharmin* (subject), yet their respective reasons (*hetu*) and examples (*udāharaṇa*) differ, while all [reasons] possess the three characteristics—namely, being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), being present in similar instances (*sapakṣe sattvam*), and being entirely absent in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣe 'sattvam*). However, these [fallacies] do not arise in mutual opposition.

Regarding this correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*), both schools are hesitant and unable to resolve it into a single tenet; therefore, it is termed the "inconclusive fallacy of contradictory certainty" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*).

Now, although the "color established by ultimate reality" (*paramārthasiddharūpa*) is a common property (*dharmin*) subject to dispute, the reason (*hetu*) is nonetheless common (rather than distinct for each side).

Furthermore, each lacks the third characteristic (*rūpa*) [of the middle term]—namely, the "pervasion in the dissimilar instance" (*vipakṣavyāvṛtti*)—and thus does not possess all three characteristics (*trirūpa*). Consequently, it is not certain.

This is the fallacy of the inconclusive contradictory (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*). Question: Since this fallacy does not exist, why does the *Hetuvidyā-ṭīkā* state that one commits the fallacy of the "contradictory certainty regarding the specific characteristic of the property" (*dharmasvalakṣaṇaviruddhāvyabhicārin*)?
Answer: This is merely the result of the author of the commentary writing impulsively; it is derived from the previously mentioned "inconclusive common" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) fallacy.
It appears to be the fallacy of the "contradictory certainty regarding the specific characteristic of the property," but it is not truly so.
The above constitutes the first part of the explanation of the "correct cause" (*samyag-hetu*): the direct explanation and the analysis of the meaning, which are now complete.

△ Third, the conclusion: Because this "object-cause" exists, one must establish the phrase "that which is included in the first three [categories] but not included by the eye" as the reason (*hetu*), thereby mutually eliminating faults such as the "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) and the "contradictory" (*viruddha*).
The above concludes the explanation of the correct reason (*saddhetu*). △ Second, the explanation of the provisional statement used to eliminate faults.
Next, regarding the clarification of the provisional statement for eliminating faults: Question: What is the purpose of the initial self-admitted statement? Answer:

Because within the formal arguments (*pramāṇa*) established by the Three Piṭakas, one generally commits the fault of "contradiction with a specific property of the subject" (*dharmiviśeṣaviruddha*). This is because, according to the principles of *Hetuvidyā* (Logic), if a formal argument contains a fault...

[The opponent] uses the phrase "admittedly" (*abhyupagama*) to exclude [this fault]. Now, since the inference of the Tripiṭaka master contains this fallacy of "contradiction regarding the qualification of the subject" (*dharmiviśeṣaviruddha*), he specifically employs the term "admittedly" at the outset to exclude it. Question: How can such a fallacy occur? Answer:

It is because within the subject of the Tripiṭaka master’s inference, although the word is not explicitly attached, the meaning is implicitly intended (*antarbhūta*). This is because the Mahāyāna school maintains two distinct positions.

Regarding form (*rūpa*): there is form that is essentially separate from visual consciousness (namely, the *nimitta-bhāga* of the eighth consciousness), and there is form that is not separate from the *nimitta-bhāga* of visual consciousness (namely, that which is produced by visual consciousness itself).
If it is form separate from visual consciousness, the Hīnayāna schools accept it; if it is form not separate from visual consciousness, the Hīnayāna schools do not accept it.
Now, the Tripiṭaka Master’s formal inference (*pramāṇa*) states: "True and universally established form" is the subject (*dharmin*). If we consider its verbal expression:

Regarding the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*): this is color (*rūpa*) as admitted by both the proponent and the opponent, and it cites the reason that "it is included within the first three [elements] but not included within the eye.
This merely establishes that the color admitted by both is not separate from visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).

If one considers the position intended by the Tripiṭaka masters, they merely establish that the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) color is not separate from visual consciousness, using the reason that "it is included within the first three but not included within the eye" to establish the *dharmin* (the subject).

Regarding the distinction between the intended meaning (*abhiprāya*) and the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*): color-form (*rūpa*) is certainly not separated from visual consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*). Therefore, the *Yinming shu* (Commentary on Logic) states:
"That which is 'truly established' as color-form is the self-characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) of the subject (*dharmin*).

That 'color-form is certainly not separated from visual consciousness' is the self-characteristic of the property (*dharma*). 'Color-form is certainly separated from visual consciousness' is not [the case]; it is the specific characteristic of the subject intended by the proponent."
"Granted (this is so). This is not separate from eye-consciousness and form (or ear-consciousness). Question:

When the opponent has exposed the fault of contradiction with the established doctrine (*dharmasiddha*) regarding the valid cognition of the Tripiṭaka, how can the words "self-granted" (*svābhyupagama*) serve as a refutation? Answer:

When the opponent presents a syllogism that contradicts [the established doctrine], one uses the two characters "self-granted" to expose the opponent's syllogism as committing the fallacy of the "uncertain" (*anaikāntika*) reason within a common locus (*sādhāraṇa*). Since the opponent's syllogism already carries this internal fault, furthermore...
By what reasoning can it be shown that there is the fault of contradiction regarding the specific characteristics of the *dharmin* within the measure of the Three Pitakas?

Question: What is the manner in which the Hīnayāna presents this contradiction with the valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? Answer: The Hīnayāna says: At first glance, the proponent’s statement expresses the specifically characterized (*svalakṣaṇa*) [referring to the color established by consensus];

thus, the three members [of the syllogism] are without fault. However, upon investigating that which is established, it is fundamentally the "concealed" [referring to the aspectual color, *nimittabhāga-rūpa*]. If, with respect to the *dharmin*...

Regarding the distinction of the mental faculty (*manas*), in order to establish through an analogy that the "aspect-color" (*nimitta-rūpa*) admitted by the proponent as existing upon the subject (*dharmin*) is not separate from eye-consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*), the eye-consciousness itself cannot serve as the corroborative example (*sapakṣa*).

For instance, just as there is no eye-consciousness that is not separated from [objective] color (*rūpa*), because all objective colors are separated from eye-consciousness, once they are separated, the eye-consciousness cannot serve as the corroborative example. Thus...

This constitutes a counter-example (*vipakṣa*). That is, the reason (*hetu*)—namely, "being the first three," and so forth—is applied instead to the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), which serves as the counter-example.

Therefore, the treatise states: "Where there is no locus for the similar class (*sapakṣa*), the thesis (*pakṣa*) of the proponent is not established; where there is a locus for the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), it conversely establishes the contradictory thesis-meaning of the opponent.
Thus, the reason (*hetu*) established by the non-revising Hīnayāna school is set forth as a proof of contradiction (*viruddhahetu*), stating: "Because it is truly established [as its own nature]."

Form (*rūpa*) is an existent phenomenon (*dharma*). It is not the case that it is not inseparable from visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*); this is our thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: because it is included among the first three [bases] (*āyatana*) while not being included by the eye.

The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is, for instance, visual consciousness (since visual consciousness apprehends its object through separation and is therefore not non-separate from form). The application (*upanaya*) states:

all things that are included among the first three bases while not being included by the eye are not non-separate from visual consciousness, just like the example of visual consciousness (which is separate from external form). As for the word "not" (*na*), it negates [the opposite].

It is non-existent. The Hīnayāna school claims that there is no form (*rūpa*) that is not separated from eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). This immediately negates the intended meaning of the Tripiṭaka Master, who maintains that the "aspect-part" (*nimittabhāga*) of form is non-existent.

For this reason, the Tripiṭaka Master intentionally included the phrase "as he himself admits" (*svābhyupagama*) to take the forms of Buddhas in other directions and apply them as an "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) fallacy against the opponent's formal argument (*prayoga*).
He states the refutation: "Is it like the case where eye-consciousness is the first of the three [consciousnesses]?"
[The object] is subsumed by the eye, yet not subsumed by the eye [as a physical organ].
Is it not the case that you have proven that the "color" (rūpa) which you maintain to be established [as an external object] is not separate from the color that is the object of visual consciousness?

Is it not like my own position, where the color of a Buddha in another realm—though subsumed by the first three [elements] and not subsumed by the eye [organ]—is nonetheless a color that is not separate from the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of visual consciousness?
[If you reply: "But have you not [already] established that the 'form' (rūpa) which is universally acknowledged (prasiddha) by you is nonetheless inseparable from visual consciousness?

[In that case], since the opponent's formal argument (sādhana) commits the fallacy of the "uncertainty for another" (anyatarāsiddhi) within a common locus, it is clearly known that this is not a genuine refutation (dūṣaṇa). [Since it is not a genuine refutation, then...]
The Tripitaka Master, however, has truly established a valid proof (*sādhana*). Question:

If one does not state "admitted by oneself" regarding the reason, what is wrong with using the physical form of a Buddha from another world-system as a probans provided by the opponent to establish a fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) against the externalist? Answer:

If one were to use the physical form of a Buddha from another world-system without stating it is "admitted by oneself," then since the followers of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) do not admit it, one would commit the fallacy of being "partially accepted by the opponent" (*ekadeśa-parasiddha*).

First, there is the fallacy of *anyatarāsiddha* (unestablished for one party). This is because the opponent does not admit that the physical form (*rūpa*) of a Buddha from another realm is included within the first three [realms] or among the causes not apprehended by the eye.

Therefore, the *Hetuvidyā-ṭīkā* states: "If one does not specify 'admitted by oneself,' then one cannot use the physical form of a Buddha from another realm as an instance of *anaikāntika* (inconclusive);
for such a statement would then incur the fallacy of being unestablished for one party. Question: Why does it not wait for the opponent to state [this]?

After [the opponent] has contradicted the valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), why is it necessary to pre-emptively attach the phrase "as admitted by oneself" (*svīkṛta*)? Answer: Fearing that it might be difficult at the time [of debate], one provides this defense beforehand.

The first section, explaining the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*), is concluded. II. Presenting the Questions and Answers (in three parts): 1. Distinguishing the basis of the thesis (*pakṣāśraya*). 2. Distinguishing the thesis and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Third, the establishment [of the thesis] is explained.

First, regarding the initial presentation of the question and answer: first, the question. The two characters "because it is real" (*tattvataḥ*) have already excluded the fault of contradicting scripture.

Why, then, is the term "universally acknowledged" (*prasiddha*) not attached to the subject (*pakṣa*) presented previously? Furthermore, there would be the fault of contradicting one's own tenets. Answer: Regarding the two characters "because it is real": [the term "universally acknowledged" is not required].

This merely excludes the fault of contradicting the teaching regarding the essential nature (*pakṣa-svarūpa*) of the thesis; it does not exclude the contradiction of the thesis regarding its substratum (*pakṣāśraya*).
The two characters "universally established" (*prasiddha*) serve precisely to exclude faults such as contradicting the thesis regarding its substratum.
Both the worldly perspective and the teachings of the Hīnayāna maintain that form is distinct from visual consciousness.

Therefore, the two terms "because of the eye" and "because of [form]" are used to exclude the fault of contradicting the scriptural authority regarding the thesis and its nature. Within the *dharmin* (the locus) upon which the thesis depends, there are inherently two kinds of form that are not universally established (*aprasiddha*).

If one were to arbitrarily establish these as the *dharmin*, it would contradict the thesis that form is not separate from visual consciousness; thus, it is necessary to employ what is universally established...
The two characters "cheng" (established) serve as a concise abbreviation. △ Second, the analysis of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Question:
What is the distinction between the visual consciousness in the *uttarapakṣa* (the latter member of the syllogism) and the visual consciousness in the homologous example (*sapakṣa*)? Answer:

Although the visual consciousness mentioned in the *uttarapakṣa* is nominally the same, one must understand that their intended meanings (*abhiprāya*) are distinct. The visual consciousness in the *uttarapakṣa* is intended to mean the self-cognizing aspect (*svasaṃvedanabhāga*). The visual consciousness in the homologous example... [is intended to mean the object-cognizing aspect].

The visual consciousness within the analogy is accepted as the *darśana-bhāga* (seeing portion). This is because the *darśana-bhāga* is not separate from the *svasaṃvedana-bhāga* (self-verifying portion), just as in our own school the *nimitta-bhāga* (image portion) is not separate from the *svasaṃvedana-bhāga*.
Question: If that is so, why not formulate the syllogism as follows? "The *nimitta-bhāga* is the subject (*dharmin*);
it is necessarily not separate from the *svasaṃvedana-bhāga* is the thesis (*pakṣa*); the reason (*hetu*) is: 'because it is subsumed under the first three [bases] and is not seen by the eye'."

Because it is subsumed [within the same category]. It is analogous to the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*). Answer: Because the Hīnayāna does not admit four portions, and fearing the commission of faults such as "conforming to one" (*anuvartana*), it speaks only of "eye-consciousness."
△ 3. Discerning the Establishment. Question:

Regarding this statement of the measure (*pramāṇa*), what kind of form (*rūpa*) is established? Answer: If one considers only the verbal expression, then neither of the two kinds of forms—the aspect (*ākāra*) nor the substance (*svabhāva*)—can be established.
However, if one applies the intention to the words, then the aspect-form (*ākāra-rūpa*) is established. Furthermore...
Explanation: If, prior to the Small Vehicle’s inquiry, one establishes [the position] by applying the words to the intended meaning;
yet, once the Small Vehicle has inquired and the Mahāyāna has responded, one may then establish it by applying the intended meaning (the admitted aspect-part) to the words.

To conform the words to the intended meaning: this means that while the intended meaning accepts that [the object] is fundamentally the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect), the verbal expression can only state that it is "matter" (*rūpa*).

To conform the intended meaning to the words: this means that although the verbal expression only mentions "matter," the intended meaning’s acceptance of it as the *nimittabhāga* is already established.

Question: Since you have already divided color into two types—the aspect (nimitta-bhāga) and the objective essence (svabhāva)—this is not universally established (*aprasiddha*). Therefore, why do you state in the prior proposition that it is "universally established color" (*prasiddha-rūpa*)?
For the aspect is not commonly accepted [as such]. Answer: If one considers the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the subject (*dharmin*) as it is expressed in words, then [it is indeed so].

Since "form" (rūpa) is accepted by both the proponent and the opponent, the two characters "extremely established" (ji cheng) are applied. If the form of the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) is merely that which is accepted within the Mahāyāna system, how could it relate to the verbal expression of its own-characteristic (svalakṣaṇa)?
How, then, could there be a lack of universal establishment? As for the commentaries all stating that one must not separate [the two], this is incorrect.
If that were so, then while the Hīnayāna would maintain that the Buddha possesses contaminated (sāsrava) form, the Mahāyāna would maintain that the Buddha possesses uncontaminated (anāsrava) form.
If form and so forth were already present before one, would they not—were they not distinguished—be called "universally established form"?
Since that is not the case, how could this be?

If it is said that those two schools do not mutually admit the existence of form (*rūpa*), and since this must necessarily be distinguished [from the other], then how can these two types—the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) and the *svabhāva-bhāga* (essential nature)—not be distinguished?
The second major section, which correctly elucidates [the argument], is hereby concluded.
△ Third, the concluding praise.
Question: Now you discuss the school and manifest the nature (*dharmatā*). Why do you extensively cite texts on the three-membered syllogism (*trirūpa-anumāna*)? Answer:

Even when the Buddhas preach the Dharma, they must still rely upon conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) (not discarding the conventional to exclusively explain the ultimate). How much more so in the case of this three-membered syllogism!

Its principles permeate the five sciences (*pañca-vidyā-sthāna*—namely, inner science, logic, grammar, medicine, and the arts and crafts); it is not merely a matter of words and language, but takes refutation and establishment as its primary aim, generating wisdom through speech.

Taking thorough understanding as its essence (it is possible), it can crush the divergent attachments of ordinary beings and the Small Vehicle, thereby establishing the fundamental principles of the Buddha-dharma.

Thus, the teaching would not be perfect for those lacking wisdom—just as, for example, wood is not straight without a string. Now that this has been compared (then), one can give rise to sincere faith and subdue the deluded and inverted doubts;
furthermore, when measured (then), one can determine the true exposition and block the [delusions of] the wild and ignorant.
By refuting false doctrines, the wheel of the True Dharma is set in perpetual motion, and the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) is widely propagated.

Thus, one knows that phenomena possess the power to manifest principles, and words possess the force to establish the definitive truth. As the Great Master Ci'en said: "The *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* (Treatise on Logic)..."
Originally, these were spoken solely by the Buddha; however, the texts are extensive and the meanings are dispersed throughout the various scriptures.

Thus, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* states: "When a bodhisattva seeks the Dharma, where should they seek it? They should seek it within all five fields of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*). One seeks the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*) in order to refute false arguments and establish the correct path.
At the beginning of the kalpa, Akṣapāda first delineated the categories of the real and the apparent; subsequently, Vasubandhu restated these principles.

Thus, although the fundamental principles have been set forth, their profound subtleties remain undifferentiated; consequently, even when host and guest engage in mutual exposition, there is still uncertainty regarding the rules for establishing and refuting arguments.
There was the Bodhisattva Dignāga, who was renowned as one of the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa destined to appear in this world.

He concealed his traces among the crags and marshes, dwelling upon the mountain peaks in meditative equipoise (*samādhi*). He examined the merits and defects of literary compositions and scrutinized the complexity or conciseness of their phrasing and meaning.

At that time, the mountain valleys resounded with a roar and the clouds and mists shifted their colors; the mountain deity lifted the Bodhisattva’s feet, holding them aloft at a height of a hundred *chi*.

He proclaimed: "The Buddha taught that the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*) is profound and subtle, difficult to fathom. Since the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, its great meaning has been lost and its transmission severed.

Now, fortunately, Bhadraruci is far-reaching in his wisdom and has deeply penetrated the sacred intent; he is well-versed in the path of the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra*. We pray that you will request him to propagate it once again.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva emitted a divine light that illuminated those whose faculties were ready for conversion. At that time, King Ādityasena of Andhra in South India beheld this emission of light.

Suspecting that he had entered the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) and was seeking to realize the fruit of arhatship, the Bodhisattva said: "I have entered this concentration for the purpose of observing and about to expound the profound sūtras;
my heart is set upon great enlightenment, not on aspiring for a minor fruit. The King replied, "The fruit of arhatship is that which all the noble ones look up to with reverence."
"May Your Honor swiftly realize [enlightenment]. The Bodhisattva patted him, wishing to fulfill the King's request. Then, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī snapped his fingers to rouse him, saying:
"Why do you abandon the Great Mind and instead give rise to a minor aspiration? To bring about vast benefit, you should turn the *Yoga* treatises spoken by Maitreya to rectify the collapsing order.
You may compose a work on *Hetuvidyā* (Logic) to re-establish the standards. Dignāga respectfully accepted this instruction.
I received these instructions and applied them with diligent practice. Thereupon, I contemplated deeply and refined my understanding, composing the *Nyāyamukha-śāstra* (The Gateway to Reasoning).
"Reasoning" (*nyāya*) refers to the essential nature and meaning of all phenomena; "gateway" (*mukha*) refers to the means by which one weighs and illuminates understanding.

Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* asks: "What is called the locus of reasoning (*hetuvidyā-sthāna*)? It is all matters pertaining to the investigation of meanings. This is precisely what is meant here.

The dharma that constitutes the established thesis is called the "investigation of meaning. The dharma that serves as the conforming reason is called "all existing phenomena" (vastu). Within this [context]:
All matters whatsoever are *hetuvidyā* (logic), because by means of this as a cause, one is able to illuminate and examine their meaning.

For example, if non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) maintain that sound is eternal, how could they be refuted of this attachment unless it were refuted by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through inference?

As the non-Buddhists formulate an inference: "Sound" is the subject (*dharmin*); "it is necessarily eternal" is the thesis (*pakṣa*); "because it is produced" is the reason (*hetu*); the similar example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is like...
Space. Since space is not of the nature of being produced (*kṛtaka*), the reason does not apply to it; thus, the analogy is dissimilar, and the thesis that sound is permanent is not established.
According to the Buddha’s teaching, sound is impermanent. To formulate the syllogism: "Sound" is the subject (*dharmin*).
The thesis is that "all conditioned things are impermanent. The reason is: "because they are produced. The similar example is like a jar or a basin; the dissimilar example is like space and so forth.
One should know that if this means of valid cognition did not exist, how could one manifest the correct and subdue the heterodox? Therefore, on the level of the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*),...

Not receiving a single speck of dust, yet within the gateway of Buddha-activities not abandoning a single dharma—if one wishes to learn the skillful means of all Buddhas, one must fully possess the universal conduct of a Bodhisattva;
only by penetrating and clarifying each and every aspect can one bring about the great transformation.
The above concludes the eulogy of the three branches. From here below is a general eulogy of the *ālayavijñāna*; it is not a formal conclusion of the *hetuvidyā* (logic).

As extensively cited above, the textual passages concerning the *ālayavijñāna* are elucidated by the patriarchs and Buddhas and established by both the sūtras and the śāstras as the eighth fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).

Suchness and the one mind are vast and boundless; their essential nature is subtle and refined. They reveal the source of the mind as being without exterior and encompass the treasury of nature with universal penetration.
They hold the name of "repository of seeds" and act as the sovereign of total retribution. They establish the substance of sentient beings and provide the cause for nirvana.
Abiding in the initial stage, they are collectively termed *ālaya*; reaching the ultimate fruit, they are called solely "the stainless."

It prepares the ground of wisdom for both this and future lives, and establishes the gateway to benefit for oneself and others. Depending on whether there is grasping or non-grasping, it assumes many names;

based on defiled or pure conditions, it manifests as various entities. It nurtures all things like the vast void that encompasses everything, and it brings forth the myriad dharmas like the great earth that gives birth to all.
Thus, what dharma is not subsumed? What gate is not entered? It is only because of delusion...

Taking the understanding of the single truth as the second contemplation: first, through the mind capable of discernment arising from awakened clarity, the phenomena of internal and external defilements are initiated.

From within that one perfect stillness, the faculties and objects are differentiated; the four great elements within are gathered to form the body, while the four great elements without are manifested as the environment.
Internally, consciousness and emotion become defilements; externally, perceptions and appearances constitute the dust of the senses. Without thought...
The objective realm penetrates the single suchness; though there are perceptions, the truth manifests as ten thousand distinctions.

If one can dissolve the mind into the *dharmadhātu* and open the realm to reveal true emptiness, illusory obscurations will vanish entirely and the single path will manifest clearly. This may be called tearing apart the fine mesh of the path of delusion and unlocking the heavy bolts of the gate of awakening.
When the昏夢 (drowsy dream) awakens, great enlightenment is ever-luminous; when the狂性 (mad nature) ceases, the original head reveals itself.
This clearly elucidates the single school of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra). One must investigate and understand it thoroughly so as to integrate it into the state of mind and its objects.

The text is easy to comprehend and need not be further explained. The profound intent behind this concluding praise is to lead people to realize their inherent nature through the very phenomena they encounter.
May those who study these three schools each reflect upon this.
A Brief Explanation of the Valid Cognition of True Consciousness-Only (End)
